## Claude synthesis

### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Polikoff and colleagues report a fall-2023 wave of the Understanding America Study (a probability-based, address-sampled panel; 3,905 completers, fielded September 19–October 29, 2023) in which adults rated whether 18 concrete race-related classroom topics are appropriate, separately for elementary and high school, alongside six general attitude items. The descriptive core is solid and is what the paper should be cited for: every one of the 18 topics draws majority support (56–92%) for high school while only 5 of 18 do for elementary (Figure 1, p.6); the Democrat–Republican difference on the IRT support scale is 1.03 theta points, about 1.1 SD (Table 3, Model 1, p.9); and bivariate county and state partisanship gaps (county strong Republican −0.51) collapse to near zero (−0.09) once individual party identification enters (Model 8), so place-based differences in opinion are mostly differences in who lives there. Every count the writing reviewer checked in the Results narrative matched the bar charts, and the reproducibility reviewer found that the Figure 1 values and Table 1 match the publicly posted UAS topline to the percentage point. The title's question — what *explains* the partisan gap — is answered far less securely. The "explanation" is sequential OLS with one attitude item added at a time; the "more than half" and "approximately 30% to 40%" shares on p.8 hold only against the bivariate Model 1, while the "about 25%" shares on p.10 hold only against Model 8, so no single baseline reproduces the text; Models 9–13 are estimated on roughly half the sample (N = 1,727–1,827 versus 3,892) with no explanation and no like-for-like baseline; the Discussion's "about half of the partisan gaps based on two items" (p.10) corresponds to no model in Table 3, where the two items never appear together; and the strongest "explanator" ("Children should learn about the ways White people have been racist historically in the U.S. even if that makes them feel guilty") is close to being another support item, so its absorbing the partisan coefficient says little about mechanism and does not isolate "concern about White students feeling guilty" as the abstract puts it. Add that the novelty claims are oversold (the authors' own 2024 project report had already published the high-school majorities, an IRT scale, and the guilt conjecture; the "opt-in panel" criticism on p.3 does not fit the Pew and Monmouth polls it is aimed at; the education-politics literature on partisan sorting is absent), that the sample bookkeeping on p.3 does not reconcile with the Ns in Table 3, and that the article carries no data statement, code, software, weighting, or standard-error information, and the right posture is: rely on Figures 1–2 and the Model 1 versus Model 8 comparison, always quote the fielding date, and treat the decomposition percentages, the "deep-red states" framing, and the media and policy narrative of the Discussion as hypotheses the data motivate rather than findings they establish.

#### Key Strengths

- A genuinely finer-grained instrument than anything in the prior polling: 18 behaviorally specific topics (full wording in Table 2, p.5), pretested in two rounds of cognitive interviews, asked separately for Grades K–5 and 9–12, with support ranging from 18% to 92% across items (Figure 1, p.6). The elementary/high-school contrast — 5 of 18 majorities versus 18 of 18 — is the paper's most useful new fact and is directly visible in the exhibit.
- A probability-based panel with survey weights, a stated field period, and Rao-Scott-adjusted tests for the group comparisons (pp.3, 6). For national item-level percentages this is about as good as online survey data get, and the descriptive exhibits reproduce against the public UAS topline.
- The geography decomposition is clean and citable: county and state partisanship gaps that are large bivariately (Models 3–4) are almost entirely absorbed by individual party identification (Model 8), while the partisan coefficients themselves barely move when demographics are added (−1.03 to −0.94; −0.61 to −0.52). Place is mostly composition.
- The Results narrative on pp.6–7 is faithful to Figures 1 and 2. Every count the writing reviewer checked (five elementary majorities, eight items below one-third, majority high-school support for all 18, "four of the top five," 15 of 18 majorities in strong-Republican states) matches the printed bar values.
- The authors state plainly that the attitude regressions are not causal (p.8) and that the findings are descriptive (p.10), and Table 3 reports N, R², df, F, and RMSE for all 14 models, which is what let the reviewers audit it.

#### Key Concerns

- The "share of the partisan gap explained" figures cannot be reproduced against any single baseline. Against Model 8 (Republican −0.94, Neither −0.52), the guilt item (Model 13: −0.48, −0.30) accounts for 49% and 42%, not "more than half"; the "more than half" holds only against the uncontrolled Model 1 (53%, 51%). The "about 25%" shares for Models 10 and 14 hold only against Model 8 (19–25%), not Model 1 (28–36%). The text also never says which baseline it used.
- Models 9–13 use roughly half the sample (N = 1,727–1,827 versus 3,892 in Model 8 and 3,818 in Model 14; Table 3, p.9) and the text never says why. Model 9, whose added item is null (−0.04), already moves the Republican coefficient from −0.94 to −0.88, so part of every "explained" share is sample change. No Model 8 baseline on the reduced sample is reported.
- The Discussion's headline — "we can explain about half of the partisan gaps based on two items" (p.10) — summarizes no estimate shown: the two items enter only separately (Models 12 and 13). And the stronger of them is substantively a curriculum-support item in the same agree/disagree format, so its overlap with the outcome is close to built in; it does not measure concern about guilt as distinct from opposition to the content.
- The literature positioning is oversold in ways a citing reader should know. The 2024 project report the paper describes as having "only examined partisan views" (p.2) already reported the high-school majorities, an IRT scale, and the guilt hypothesis (literature reviewer's external check); the p.3 claim that "many" of the cited polls used opt-in panels fits only the Mood of the Nation poll, not Pew's probability panel or Monmouth's telephone samples; and Houston (2024, AERJ) on partisan sorting in education opinion, plus the political-science work on partisanship shaping racial attitudes, goes unmentioned. Two supporting citations on p.10 (Strauss 2023, whose title reports Moms for Liberty candidates losing; the "nationwide" book-challenge statistic) do not support the sentences they are attached to.
- Documentation stops short of what a reader needs to audit the inferential work. The p.3 sample arithmetic does not reconcile (2,005 + 1,900 equals the 3,905 responders, not the 4,896 invited; 3,905/4,896 is 79.8%, not 81%; six regression Ns exceed 3,905). The paper never states whether regressions or figures are weighted, what standard-error estimator is used (Table 3 has stars but no SEs), how the A/B forms were placed on one IRT scale, or which category is the county reference (the "County leans Democrat" row reads 0.00 in all eight columns although df_m implies four estimated county parameters). There is no data availability statement, replication code, software statement, or survey identifier, and the online appendix carrying Table A1 (all subgroup crosstabs), the elementary regressions, and the robustness checks does not travel with the PDF.

#### What to Rely On

- Grade-level topline support, always with the fielding date: among U.S. adults in fall 2023, all 18 race-related topics had majority support as appropriate for high school (56% to 92%) and 5 of 18 did for elementary school (Figure 1, p.6). The four most-supported topics are the same at both levels (equal treatment regardless of skin color, colonists harming Native Americans, interracial marriage rights, acting out civil-rights demonstrations).
- The size of the partisan divide on the scale: Democrats average 0.47 and Republicans −0.56 on the high-school theta, a gap of 1.03 (about 1.1 SD; p.7 and Table 3 Model 1), with Independents/neither at −0.61. The "about 30 percentage points" average item gap (p.7) is consistent with the party averages the text reports (87% vs 56% high school; 56% vs 26% elementary) but its item detail is in the unavailable Table A1.
- Place is mostly composition: county and state partisanship gaps are large bivariately (county strong Republican −0.51; state leans Republican −0.31; Models 3–4) and shrink to −0.09 or less once individual party identification is added (Model 8). This is the paper's best-supported analytic claim.
- Demographic gaps are smaller than partisan ones and are mostly absorbed by partisanship: the NH Black coefficient falls from 0.34 (Model 2) to 0.12 (Model 8), the parent coefficient from −0.28 (Model 7) to −0.16 (Model 8). Note that Model 8 adds all covariates at once, so "absorbed by partisanship" is approximate.
- Five of the six attitude items are strongly associated with the support scale (all p < .001 except LeadersWht at −0.04; Models 9–14), and the guilt and minority-authors items are the two most strongly associated with the partisan gap. The qualitative ordering is robust across baselines; the percentages are not.
- The instrument itself: Table 2 gives the full wording of every topic and attitude item, and the descriptive exhibits match the public UAS topline, so the item bank can be reused or compared against.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- "Concern about White guilt explains more than half of the partisan gap" (abstract, p.8, p.10) — the share is 42–49% against the like-for-like Model 8 baseline, is computed on an unexplained half-sample, and the item bundles support for teaching about historical racism with tolerance of guilt; it is a statistical-overlap share, not a mechanism.
- "About half of the partisan gaps based on two items" (p.10) — no joint model is reported; single-item shares are not additive when the items are correlated. Do not cite this as an estimate.
- Any "explains X%" percentage quoted from the prose — recompute it from Table 3 and state the baseline; the p.8 figures use Model 1 and the p.10 figures use Model 8.
- "Opposition to most racial topics in elementary schools" (abstract) — Figure 1 shows percent agree/strongly agree with "I'm not sure" in the denominator; 13 items below 50% support is not majority opposition, and the paper never reports the disagree share.
- "Majority support for 15 of 18 topics in deep-red states" (pp.7, 10; Figure 2) — "strong Republican" means 2020 Trump share of 65% or more, which by the reviewers' external reading of certified results is about four low-population states; no group N or confidence interval is reported, each item was seen by roughly half of those respondents, and several of the 15 majorities sit at 55–58%. Directionally informative, low precision.
- The opinion–policy incongruence and Fox News arguments in the Discussion (p.10) — the survey contains no measure of media exposure and the 18 items are never mapped onto what the state restrictions actually prohibit; the cited Fox News studies concern vote share and ideological polarization, not curriculum opinion, and press accounts of the one field experiment cited report racial attitudes largely unchanged.
- The novelty framing on p.3 — the "opt-in" criticism does not fit the Pew and Monmouth polls cited; the authors' own 2024 report already carried the high-school majorities and the guilt conjecture; cite Saavedra et al. (2024) for the partisan toplines and this article for the demographic/geographic breakdowns and the decomposition.
- The demographic "controls" — Table 3 contains no age, gender, religion, region, or urbanicity variables, so "net of demographics" means net of race, income, education, parent status, and county partisanship; the parent coefficient plausibly proxies age.
- The timing — fieldwork ended October 29, 2023; the Introduction is framed around the January 2025 executive order and a March 2026 count of 20 state bans, and the paper does not discuss whether opinion has moved since.
- Anything resting on the online appendix (Table A1 crosstabs and the 51- and 48-point item gaps, elementary regressions in A2, midpoint-coding robustness in A3–A4, item-level guilt models in A5–A6, the county version of Figure 2, and the theta distributions) — none of it was available to this review.

Claims from the sub-reviews checked against the paper (page images of Figure 1, Figure 2, and Table 3 were rendered and inspected; the online appendix was not available).

- Model 13 vs Model 8 vs Model 1 partisan coefficients (−0.48/−0.30; −0.94/−0.52; −1.03/−0.61) and the implied 49%/42% vs 53%/51% shares — CONFIRMED (Table 3, p.9).
- Models 9–13 N = 1,746; 1,827; 1,784; 1,732; 1,727 vs Model 8 N = 3,892 and Model 14 N = 3,818; text silent on the drop — CONFIRMED (Table 3; pp.6–8).
- No model in Table 3 contains both LrnAbtWhtRacist and LrnAbtPOCgood — CONFIRMED; each attitude item appears in exactly one column.
- "About 25%" for Models 10 and 14 holds against Model 8 (Rep 23%, 21%; Neither 25%, 19%) but not Model 1 (30%, 28%; 36%, 31%) — CONFIRMED.
- Model 9 (LeadersWht −0.04, n.s.) shifts Republican −0.94 to −0.88 and Neither −0.52 to −0.55 — CONFIRMED.
- Regression Ns of 3,932–3,973 exceed the 3,905 responders; 2,005 + 1,900 = 3,905; 3,905/4,896 = 79.8% — CONFIRMED (p.3; Table 3). The reproducibility reviewer's external check of the UAS 567 methodology (3,974 starters, 3,905 completers) would reconcile the 81% and the Ns, but the paper itself does not — COULD NOT CHECK against the paper.
- "County leans Democrat" = 0.00 in all eight columns where county dummies appear; Model 3 df_m = 4; Model 8 df_m = 17 = 2 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 2 + 1 — CONFIRMED.
- Table 3 note "HS = Hispanic" against a row labelled "Hispanic" and Table 1's "HS = high school" — CONFIRMED.
- Note 3 says state partisanship was omitted "for Models 9 through 14," but Model 8 also has no state rows — CONFIRMED.
- Figure 1 counts: five elementary items above 50% (89, 61, 56, 53, 53); eight below one-third (30, 18, 33, 25, 28, 20, 33, 30); three lowest are sexual-assault book (18), college admissions (20), police shooting (25); all 18 high-school items above 50% (minimum 56); four of the top five shared; least-supported high-school items named at 56, 60, 62, 62 with the 65% item unnamed — CONFIRMED.
- Figure 2: 15 of 18 majorities in strong-Republican states, with 47, 45, 45 below 50; average strong-Democrat minus strong-Republican gap about 12 points, largest 25 and 24 — CONFIRMED.
- Model 1 constant 0.47 and Republican −1.03 match the reported theta means (0.47, −0.56) and difference 1.03; R² .23 consistent with RMSE 0.83 and SD 0.94 — CONFIRMED.
- Text "about 0.5 theta points lower" for Independents in Model 1 vs the table's −0.61 — CONFIRMED as a loose description (0.52 is the Model 8 value).
- Model 13 demographic coefficients "mostly unchanged": NH Black 0.12* to −0.03, NH Asian −0.10 to −0.20**, parent −0.16*** to −0.10* — CONFIRMED (the writing reviewer's "partial mismatch" is fair).
- Strauss (2023) cited for the election of curriculum-restricting board candidates while its reference-list title reads "Voters drub Moms for Liberty 'parental rights' candidates at the ballot"; Cabrera et al. (2014), whose title concerns the Tucson Mexican American Studies controversy, cited for 1990s attacks — CONFIRMED from the reference list (pp.12–13) and p.2/p.10 text.
- Abstract wording "concern about White students feeling guilty" versus the item's compound wording in Table 2 — CONFIRMED.
- The contribution reviewer's statement that the Figure 1 note says "not sure" responses count against support — CORRECTED: the note defines support as agree/strongly agree but does not state the denominator; that "not sure" remains in the denominator comes from the reproducibility reviewer's recomputation against the public topline, not from the paper.
- The contribution reviewer's uncritical relay of the paper's "81%" and "opt-in panels" statements as strengths — CORRECTED in this synthesis by the writing reviewer's arithmetic (79.8%) and the literature reviewer's check of the cited polls' sampling.
- Contents of Saavedra et al. (2024), the UAS 567 topline and methodology document, the sampling of the Pew/Monmouth/Mood of the Nation polls, Houston (2024), and press summaries of Broockman and Kalla — COULD NOT CHECK against the paper; these are the sub-reviewers' external web checks and are reported as such.
- Which 2020 states exceed 65% Trump share — COULD NOT CHECK from the paper (not stated); the reviewers' reading (WY, WV, OK, ND) is consistent with certified 2020 returns as I recall them but is external.

## Codex synthesis

### Overall Assessment: Useful With Caveats

This paper provides credible, useful descriptive evidence that Americans' stated acceptance of race-related classroom content depends on the particular activity and school level, alongside substantial partisan differences. The published estimates show majority support for all 18 high-school scenarios but only five elementary-school scenarios (p. 6, Figure 1). Its strongest contribution is this detailed mapping of preferences, supported by probability-based recruitment, survey weighting, and explicit item wording; it extends an acknowledged project report rather than independently rediscovering partisan polarization (pp. 2–5). My assessment is that these descriptive findings remain valuable despite weak reproducibility documentation. The proposed explanation of partisan differences deserves less weight: the guilt-related item combines support for historical instruction with willingness to accept possible guilt, and the attitude-adjusted regressions change samples, preventing a clean attribution of coefficient attenuation to the added attitude (p. 5, Table 2; p. 9, Table 3). Read the study as a snapshot of stated preferences during its 2023 field period (p. 3, Data), not as evidence that guilt or partisan media causes opposition, that reassurance would change views, or that particular communities endorse particular policies. Those distinctions justify useful_with_caveats rather than either unqualified reliance or rejection of the descriptive contribution.

#### Key Strengths

- The design fits the descriptive question: address-based probability recruitment, survey-specific weights, cognitive interviews, and randomized questionnaire forms and topic order support an interpretable account of stated curricular preferences (pp. 3–4). These are documented strengths, not guarantees against nonresponse or social-desirability bias.
- Full scenario wording and readable exhibits make the main contribution directly inspectable: the same broad curriculum label covers activities with markedly different levels of endorsement across school settings (p. 5, Table 2; p. 6, Figure 1). This specificity is more useful than treating race-related instruction as a single policy preference.
- The geographic comparison distinguishes respondents' personal partisanship from the political composition of their states, showing substantial high-school support even in the pooled strongly Republican state category (p. 8, Figure 2). This usefully qualifies assumptions of uniform opposition in conservative settings.
- The article acknowledges earlier project publications, provides historical context, and explicitly recognizes noncausality, possible social-desirability bias, and the gap between stated attitudes and behavior (pp. 2–3, 8, 10–11). These qualifications help readers separate its findings from its policy hypotheses.

#### Key Concerns

- The proposed explanatory attitudes partly restate curricular preferences. The historical-racism/guilt item does not separately measure an expectation that instruction causes guilt, and the minority-authors item directly endorses curricular inclusion (p. 5, Table 2). My judgment is that their overlap with the outcome limits their interpretation as distinct mechanisms, even though their reported associations are informative.
- The key regression comparisons change the estimation sample: Model 8 has N = 3,892, Model 12 has N = 1,732, and Model 13 has N = 1,727; their Republican coefficients are −0.94, −0.60, and −0.48, respectively (p. 9, Table 3). No demographic-only baselines on the attitude models' exact samples are shown, and the attitudes enter separately. The table therefore does not establish a same-sample or joint decomposition of partisan differences; planned missingness remains a possible explanation for the sample changes.
- Independent reconstruction is limited by incomplete documentation of latent-scale calibration across disjoint forms, scoring, missing responses, sample flow, and variance estimation, and by the absence of an identified executable data-and-code pathway in the supplied article (pp. 3–7, 9, 11–13). Table 3 supplies significance stars without coefficient standard errors or confidence intervals (p. 9). The online appendices are not bound into the PDF and are unavailable here; weak reproducibility documentation is not evidence that the results are false or that materials cannot exist elsewhere.
- National and local generalization require restraint. The topics were deliberately selected for potential controversy, some combine race with violence or sexual content, and the weighted sample retains demographic imbalances (pp. 4–5, Tables 1–2). The figures measure stated appropriateness, omit uncertainty intervals, and pool political-context groups; they do not establish actual behavior, student effects, or a mandate in each state (pp. 6, 8, Figures 1–2).
- The explanatory and novelty framing is stronger than the evidence warrants. The authors acknowledge noncausality but develop media, mobilization, and messaging interpretations that this survey cannot test (pp. 8, 10–11). The incremental descriptive contribution is credible; probability sampling itself is not a distinctive advance over every cited predecessor, as the cited Pew study also used probability-based panels ([Pew methodology](https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2022/10/26/parents-k-12-methodology/)).

#### What to Rely On

- Higher stated appropriateness for the presented high-school scenarios than their elementary-school counterparts, with majority support for all 18 high-school items and five elementary-school items—these are directly visible point-estimate patterns, conditional on the exact wording and survey setting (p. 5, Table 2; p. 6, Figure 1).
- A substantial partisan association in the high-school support scale that persists after demographic adjustment—the Republican coefficient is −1.03 in Model 1 and −0.94 in Model 8, relative to Democrats (p. 9, Table 3); this supports an association, not a causal effect of party identity.
- Majority point estimates for 15 of 18 high-school topics among respondents pooled across strongly Republican states—this is verified in Figure 2 and describes the pooled category, not each constituent state or Republicans alone (p. 8, Figure 2; category definition on p. 7).
- Positive reported associations of support with endorsement of minority-authored books and historical-racism instruction despite possible guilt—Table 3 supports these associations, while Table 2 establishes that the predictors are themselves normative curricular statements (pp. 5, 9).

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- Majority opposition to elementary-school topics: the abstract says 'opposition to most racial topics in elementary schools' (p. 1), whereas the results say 'The other 13 items have less than 50% support' (p. 7; p. 6, Figure 1). With an 'I’m not sure' option (p. 4), nonendorsement does not by itself establish opposition; the figure displays support only.
- Guilt as the demonstrated psychological explanation: Table 2 asks whether 'Children should learn about the ways White people have been racist historically in the U.S. even if that makes them feel guilty' (p. 5), whereas the results describe 'beliefs that these topics are associated with White students’ guilt' (p. 8). The first is a conditional curricular judgment, not a direct measure of the latter belief, and does not specify that the children are White.
- A precise share of the partisan gap explained: the text says 'more than half of the Democrat/Republican and Democrat/neither gap' (p. 8), while Table 3 reports Republican/Neither coefficients of '−1.03/−0.61' in Model 1, '−0.94/−0.52' in Model 8, and '−0.48/−0.30' in Model 13 (p. 9; significance stars omitted). Calculated from these rounded entries, attenuation is about 53%/51% against Model 1 but 49%/42% against Model 8. The claim is baseline-dependent rather than simply an arithmetic error, and changing samples prevent attributing either calculation wholly to the added attitude.
- Effects of media exposure, reassurance about guilt, or curriculum adoption on opinion or student outcomes—these are interpretations or possible interventions, not identified effects of this cross-sectional survey; the authors themselves acknowledge its descriptive nature (pp. 8, 10–11).
- Current public opinion or policy-specific local mandates—the field period precedes later events discussed in the paper (p. 3, Data; pp. 10–11), and pooled geographic estimates cannot establish a separate opinion-policy mismatch within each locality (p. 8, Figure 2).
- Claims of novelty based on earlier surveys being methodologically weak or limited to party comparisons—the paper's acknowledged antecedents establish continuity (pp. 2–3), and the cited Pew report includes probability sampling and racial/ethnic comparisons ([Pew report](https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2022/10/26/parents-differ-sharply-by-party-over-what-their-k-12-children-should-learn-in-school/)). Treat the contribution as richer topical and contextual detail, not the discovery of polarization.

#### Verification notes

- CONFIRMED — Methods/contribution: visual inspection counted majority point estimates for all 18 high-school and five elementary-school topics (p. 6, Figure 1), and 15 of 18 high-school topics in the pooled strongly Republican state category (p. 8, Figure 2).
- CONFIRMED — Methods/contribution/reproducibility: Models 8, 12, and 13 use N = 3,892, 1,732, and 1,727, with Republican coefficients −0.94, −0.60, and −0.48; the attitude predictors enter separately (p. 9, Table 3).
- CONFIRMED — Writing: recalculation supports its baseline qualification—guilt-model attenuation is about 53%/51% against Model 1 but 49%/42% against Model 8 for Republican/Neither contrasts, using the coefficients quoted above (p. 9, Table 3); the paper's 'more than half' (p. 8) is not false under every baseline.
- CONFIRMED — Writing/methods: the quoted item and prose above verify the distinction between conditional acceptance of instruction and a belief about White children's guilt (p. 5, Table 2; p. 8), and between elementary nonendorsement and opposition (p. 1; p. 6, Figure 1; p. 7).
- CONFIRMED — Writing: 'Of the 4,896 households invited, 3,905 responded, for a response rate of 81%' (p. 3, Data; no sample-flow exhibit) yields approximately 79.8% from the stated counts; this confirms the sub-review's arithmetic criticism, without establishing the intended response-rate denominator.
- COULD NOT CHECK — Methods/reproducibility: '3,905 responded' in the household account (p. 3, Data) cannot be reconciled with the 'N' of '3,973' in Model 2 from the supplied documentation (p. 9, Table 3); household-versus-person units could explain it, so the regression count is not shown to be erroneous.
- CONFIRMED — Literature: the cited Pew study used probability-based panels and reported racial/ethnic comparisons, supporting the review's narrower novelty qualification ([Pew methodology](https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2022/10/26/parents-k-12-methodology/); [Pew report](https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2022/10/26/parents-differ-sharply-by-party-over-what-their-k-12-children-should-learn-in-school/)); its other external-citation critiques were not independently rechecked and are not relied on here.
- COULD NOT CHECK — All dimensions: appendix-dependent subgroup, elementary-regression, and alternative-coding claims cannot be independently verified because the cited online appendices are not bound into the supplied PDF (pp. 7, 11); no replication was run.

## Responses

Authors of the reviewed paper, and readers who find an error in a review, can respond in the discussion thread below once it is enabled, or open an issue in the site's GitHub repository. Corrections are logged on the Corrections page with dates.
